text: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
picture: The Storyteller stands in dark, misty woods, hooded figure holding a low-lit red lantern, mood eerie; the foggy distant outline of a roadside motel shows one lit window.
sound: a faint wind through bare branches

text: I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between two towns that don't talk to each other.
picture: Long shot, night: a small run-down single-storey roadside motel in fog, a long row of identical doors, one lit window at the front office, an empty two-lane road.

text: Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
picture: The motel exterior, night: the same long, quiet row of doors, the single lit office window, fog pressing close; no sign of life.

text: The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in ink is a promise.
picture: Insert on an old leather guest book open on a worn wooden counter, fountain pen beside it, lit by a single desk lamp; columns of faded handwriting.

text: Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at two fourteen a.m. A different name every night.
picture: June stands behind the counter in grey dawn light, tired, holding a ring of keys, her finger resting under a fresh, dark blood-red ink line in the open guest book.

text: Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
picture: June sits at the motel front desk in a dimly lit office at night, seen from outside through the window, looking out into empty darkness, foggy road visible behind her, weary and isolated.

text: The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I started watching.
picture: June sits rigid at the front desk, both hands clutching her phone. The open guest book lies before her, its red ink hidden. Blackness fills the window behind her. Her face is pale, alert, and hollow with fatigue.

text: Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
picture: A wide view of the motel office from the inside. June is a small, tense figure at the desk. Outside the window, the parking lot's sodium lights strobe and gutter, throwing sickly orange pulses across the dark room.

text: At two fourteen, the pen moved.
picture: An extreme close insert on the surface of the guest book. A dark wood fountain pen lies at a slight, unnatural angle, as if nudged. The desk lamp light is dim and unsteady, casting long, trembling shadows. No hand is seen.

text: Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
picture: June's face lit by her phone's blue glow, eyes wide and locked on the screen showing a CCTV image of herself at the desk, her shoulders stiff with dread.

text: I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
picture: June's phone screen in a low-angle shot. On the screen is a grainy black-and-white security feed view. It shows the back of June's head as she sits at the desk. The rest of the dim office stretches out behind her.

text: And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
picture: The grainy CCTV image on June's phone shows her back and, inches behind her, the top of a tall, hooded figure in a wet raincoat, bent forward near her neck.

text: man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
picture: A wide 'CCTV' view from the high corner of the office. June sits at the desk. Directly behind her, the tall, skeletal figure in the dripping dark raincoat bends over her shoulder, its hooded face aimed down at the guest book, one pale hand reaching for the pen.

text: I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
picture: Extreme close-up on June's face from front, frozen in terror, eyes wide and locked ahead, refusing to turn; shadows creep at the edges of frame.

text: When the lights came back, the office was empty.
picture: Extreme close-up on the dark green uniform polo shirt and name badge in the foreground, the empty, shadowy motel office visible beyond the counter; a cone of white light from the desk lamp falls on vacancy.

text: The book was open. The ink was still wet.
picture: Close insert on the guest book, the open page showing one fresh, slick line in a shocking crimson pool of ink spelling out 'June Marsh, Room 6'; the handwriting is an angular cursive distinct from June's; a puddle of dark water sits on the faded wood counter beside it.

text: Room six. Two fourteen a.m. And the name was mine.
picture: June faces the open book on the counter, her back to camera; her pale face is a profile in stark horror as she stares down at her own name; the red ink gleams under the light.

text: Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
picture: Wide shot of the motel office at dawn; gray light filters through the blinds. Mr. Pell stands behind the counter, his thin frame bent over the open book, deep-set eyes fixed on the red line; he reads with a profound and weary sadness.

text: Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
picture: Medium shot from June's side as Mr. Pell reaches toward a wooden board of key hooks; his wrinkled hand, in focus, selects a single, heavy, old-fashioned brass key on a frayed red tag; the other hooks are empty.

text: "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."
picture: Mr. Pell, his face full of paternal, sorrowful finality, holds the brass key out across the dark wood counter toward the blurred, out-of-focus foreground where June stands; the guest book lies open beside his hand.

text: The Wayside Motel is still open. The night desk is always staffed. And if you sign the book, check the name above yours.
picture: The Storyteller in the hollow, his face solemn and grim in the red glow of the lantern he holds low; far behind him in the thick fog, the silhouette of a dark, endless row of motel doors stretches away, one door agape with a dim, sickly light from within.
sound: a distant door creaks on its hinges
